tool.name: RandomSampleArrayGenerator

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/geometric-tools/random-sample-array-generator.html
Generates randomly placed arrays of sampling points -- the standard field design of multiple sampling stations per plot -- inside polygon features, along polyline features, within the data cells of an integer raster with an attribute table, or in a plain extent. Each array (a grid of rows and columns, a triangular lattice filling a circle, a circle of evenly spaced points, or a one-dimensional array along a polyline) is built around a randomly placed focal location using the Random Point Generator's stratified sampling design. Counts, the minimum distance between arrays, and the minimum distance from the boundary all refer to the arrays -- footprints, nearest points, never centers. Arrays can be required to fit entirely inside the area or allowed to extend beyond it; the full array is generated either way. An optional seed makes runs exactly reproducible. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
The companion of the Random Point Generator: the same areas of interest, the same stratified sampling design, the same reproducibility seed -- but each sample is an array of points built around a randomly placed focal location, the standard design when every plot carries multiple sampling stations. If you ask for 4 arrays of 25 points each, the sample count is 4.
Area of interest. Polygons (selections honored, holes respected), polylines, an integer raster with an attribute table (NoData excluded), or a plain extent. For polygons, rasters and extents the focal location is drawn uniformly by area and the array is built around it. For polylines the focal location is drawn uniformly along the lines, and the array either surrounds it in two dimensions (grid, triangular, circular) or runs along the line itself (the one-dimensional shape below).
Array shapes: • Grid: rows x columns at a point spacing, in a square pattern. Every point carries its Row and Col (1-based; row 1 is north, column 1 west at zero orientation). • Triangular: the requested number of points on a triangular lattice, taken in order of increasing distance from the focal point (ties resolved by azimuth, so seeds reproduce exactly) -- with many points the array fills a circle. Point 1 is the focal point itself. • Circular: points evenly spaced on a circle of the given radius -- 12 points at 100 m sit 30 degrees apart, each 100 m from the focal point. The first point lies due north unless the random starting angle option spins the whole ring by a random fraction of one step. The center point can be included as a sample point, in which case it counts toward the point total (12 points = the center plus 11 on the circle). Each point carries its Bearing. • Along the polyline (polylines only): a one-dimensional array of points at a fixed interval along the line, centered on the focal location -- an odd count puts a point exactly there, an even count straddles it. The walk continues straight through junctions it passes; when it reaches the end of a line where more than one continuation exists (a Y confluence) one branch is picked and a warning reports how many arrays did so; a dead end that cuts the array short rejects the placement, and the tool draws a new focal location instead.
Orientation (grid and triangular): a fixed angle (degrees clockwise from north; at zero a grid's columns run north-south), a fresh random angle for every array, or -- on polylines -- aligned to the local line direction, so the rows run along the stream or transect the array sits on. Circular arrays are direction-free; their randomization is the starting angle above.
Point numbering as a treatment ID. Point_ID normally follows the array's geometry (grids row by row, triangular arrays outward from the focal point, circles around from the starting angle) -- so if Point_ID doubles as a treatment ID, every treatment sits at the same position in every array, confounding treatment effects with position effects (edge stations, the center, the north corner). Check Randomize the point numbering within each array to make each array's Point_ID values a fresh random permutation of 1..n instead (reproducible with the seed): assigning treatments by Point_ID is then a properly randomized block design -- the same treatments in every array, at freshly randomized stations. Row/Col and Bearing still describe the geometric position; Point_ID 1 is then no longer the focal or center point.
Everything refers to the arrays, not the points inside them. The sampling method and allocation counts count arrays. The minimum distance between arrays is measured between their nearest points (footprints -- two arrays can never approach closer than this anywhere), and on polylines it can be measured spatially, along the line, or through the connected network, exactly as in the Random Point Generator. The minimum distance from the area boundary applies to every point of the array.
When an array does not fit. With Entire array must fit checked (the default), a placement whose array would leave the polygon, land on NoData cells, or run off the end of a line is rejected and a new focal location is drawn -- every delivered array is complete, which most ecological designs require for consistent sampling. Unchecked, arrays may extend beyond the area of interest (the full array is still generated; raster points beyond the data carry a null Category, and the boundary-distance constraint no longer applies). The Advanced placement-attempts budget (always available) bounds how hard the tool tries per array before accepting a shortfall -- and a design that cannot possibly fit (an array wider than the polygon, raster or line network can hold) is detected up front and reported immediately, without consuming the budget at all.
Stratified sampling follows the Random Point Generator exactly: strata are individual polygons or polylines, raster categories, contiguous raster regions, or groups sharing a strata ID value; array counts are allocated equally, proportionally to stratum area or length, from a population field, or by density (arrays per acre, hectare, square kilometer... or per length of line). Geodesic areas and lengths make the allocation honest in any coordinate system, and geographic data is handled in an automatic equal-area working projection -- arrays are built in true meters and written back in the input coordinate system.
Output: a point feature class with Array_ID, Point_ID (the sequence within its array), Row/Col (grids), Bearing (circles), and the usual Stratum, Src_FID and Category fields where they apply. The random seed makes runs exactly reproducible -- cite it in a methods section.

param.name: boundary
param.displayname: Area of interest (polygons, polylines, or an integer raster with an attribute table; optional -- else the extent below)

dialogReference.para: The area of interest: polygons, polylines to place arrays along, or an integer raster with an attribute table (NoData excluded). Selections are honored. Leave blank to use the extent parameter instead.

param.name: extent
param.displayname: Extent (used when no area of interest is given; the Extent environment clips polygon areas)

dialogReference.para: A plain rectangular area, used when no area of interest is given.

param.name: strata_method
param.displayname: Sampling method (how the strata are defined)

dialogReference.para: How the strata are defined:

bulletList.bullet_item: None: the whole area is one stratum.
Each individual polygon or polyline is a stratum.
Each contiguous raster region: cells of one value connected by shared edges.
Groups sharing a strata ID value.

dialogReference.para: The choices are phrased to match the input. Identical to the Random Point Generator.

param.name: strata_field
param.displayname: Strata ID field (integer or text; polygons, polylines, or a raster attribute-table field)

dialogReference.para: The integer or text field whose values group features or raster categories into strata. The ObjectID field also qualifies.

param.name: alloc_method
param.displayname: Sample count allocation method (counts are ARRAYS, not points)

dialogReference.para: How many arrays each stratum receives: an equal count, a count proportional to stratum area (or length), a count equal to or proportional to a population field, or a density of arrays. The counts are arrays -- 4 arrays of 25 points each is a count of 4.

param.name: n_arrays
param.displayname: Number of sample arrays (the total, spread across the strata)

dialogReference.para: The overall number of arrays, distributed across the strata (proportional methods) or the whole area.

param.name: n_per_stratum
param.displayname: Number of sample arrays per stratum

dialogReference.para: The number of arrays each stratum receives (equal-count allocation).

param.name: population_field
param.displayname: Population field (non-negative; per feature, or a raster attribute-table field)

dialogReference.para: A non-negative numeric field driving the equal-to or proportional-to population allocations.

param.name: density
param.displayname: Density: arrays per unit (area unit; length unit for polylines)

dialogReference.para: How many arrays per unit, e.g. 0.1 arrays per square kilometer. Counts come from geodesic areas and lengths.

param.name: density_units
param.displayname: Density unit

dialogReference.para: The unit the density refers to: Acre, Square Mile, Hectare or Square Kilometer for areas; Foot, Mile, Meter or Kilometer of line length for polylines.

param.name: array_shape
param.displayname: Array shape

dialogReference.para: The design of each array:

bulletList.bullet_item: Grid: rows x columns at a point spacing (square pattern).
Triangular: n points on a triangular lattice in order of increasing distance from the focal point -- large n fills a circle.
Circular: n points evenly spaced on a circle of the given radius, optionally including the center point.
Along the polyline (polylines only): a one-dimensional array of points at a fixed interval along the line, centered at the focal location.

param.name: n_rows
param.displayname: Number of rows (grid)

dialogReference.para: Grid arrays: the number of rows. Row 1 is the northernmost at zero orientation.

param.name: n_cols
param.displayname: Number of columns (grid)

dialogReference.para: Grid arrays: the number of columns. Column 1 is the westernmost at zero orientation.

param.name: array_points
param.displayname: Number of points in each array

dialogReference.para: Triangular, circular and along-the-line arrays: how many points each array contains. For circular arrays with the center point included, the center counts -- 12 points = the center plus 11 on the circle.

param.name: point_spacing
param.displayname: Spacing between points in the array

dialogReference.para: The distance between neighboring points within each array (grid, triangular and along-the-line shapes), in the units below.

param.name: radius
param.displayname: Circle radius (points sit on this circle around the focal point)

dialogReference.para: Circular arrays: every point sits exactly this far from the focal point, in the units below.

param.name: orientation_mode
param.displayname: Array orientation (grid and triangular)

dialogReference.para: How each array is oriented:

bulletList.bullet_item: Fixed orientation angle: every array at the angle below.
Random orientation for each array: a fresh random angle per array.
Align each array to the polyline direction (polylines only): rows run along the line at the focal location.

param.name: orientation_angle
param.displayname: Orientation angle (degrees clockwise from north; at 0 a grid's columns run north-south)

dialogReference.para: The fixed rotation of every array, degrees clockwise from north. At zero a grid's columns run north-south and its rows east-west.

param.name: randomize_start
param.displayname: Random starting angle for the first point on the circle (otherwise it lies due north of the center)

dialogReference.para: Circular arrays: spin the whole ring by a random fraction of one step, so the first point falls anywhere within the first step (e.g. between 0 and 30 degrees for 12 points) instead of due north. The seed controls the spin.

param.name: include_center
param.displayname: Include the center point as a sample point (it counts toward the number of points)

dialogReference.para: Circular arrays: also place a sample point at the focal location itself (the classic center-plus-satellites cluster plot). The center counts toward the number of points: 12 points = the center plus 11 on the circle.

param.name: randomize_ids
param.displayname: Randomize the point numbering within each array (each array's Point_ID values become a random permutation of 1..n, e.g. for use as a randomized treatment ID)

dialogReference.para: Checked: each array's Point_ID values become a fresh random permutation of 1..n (reproducible with the seed), so Point_ID can serve as a randomized treatment ID -- unchecked, a treatment keyed to Point_ID would sit at the same geometric position in every array, confounding treatments with position effects. Row/Col and Bearing still describe the geometric position; Point_ID 1 is then no longer the focal or center point.

param.name: must_fit
param.displayname: Entire array must fit inside the area of interest (uncheck to let arrays extend beyond it; the full array is generated either way)

dialogReference.para: Checked (the default): a placement whose array would leave the polygon, land on NoData, or run off the end of a line is rejected and redrawn -- every delivered array is complete. Unchecked: arrays may extend beyond the area of interest; the full array is still generated (raster points beyond the data carry a null Category), and the boundary-distance constraint below no longer applies.

param.name: min_spacing
param.displayname: Minimum distance between arrays (between their nearest points, not centers; optional)

dialogReference.para: No two arrays will approach closer than this anywhere -- the distance is between their nearest points (footprints), never between centers.

param.name: spacing_type
param.displayname: How the minimum distance is measured (polylines only)

dialogReference.para: Polylines only: the between-array distance as an absolute spatial distance, a distance along the polyline (arrays on separate lines never block each other), or a network distance through connected lines -- the same three choices as the Random Point Generator.

param.name: boundary_gap
param.displayname: Minimum distance between the arrays and the area boundary (applies to every array point; optional, and only when the array must fit)

dialogReference.para: Every point of every array stays at least this far inside the boundary (from polygon edges and holes; from NoData/edge cells on rasters; measured along the line beyond the array's end points on polylines). Available only when the entire array must fit.

param.name: linear_units
param.displayname: Units for the distances above (point spacing, radius, and the two minimum distances)

dialogReference.para: Units for the point spacing, the circle radius, and the two minimum distances: Meters, Kilometers, Feet or Miles.

param.name: random_seed
param.displayname: Random seed (optional -- same seed, same arrays)

dialogReference.para: Optional: the same seed with the same inputs reproduces the same arrays exactly. Leave blank for a fresh draw each run.

param.name: max_attempts
param.displayname: Placement attempts per array before giving up (containment rejections and spacing conflicts both consume attempts)

dialogReference.para: Advanced: how many candidate focal locations each array may consume before the tool gives up on reaching the full count (default 1000). Containment rejections (the array must fit) and between-array spacing conflicts both consume attempts. Raise it to push harder in tight areas.

param.name: out_fc
param.displayname: Output point feature class

dialogReference.para: The output point feature class: Array_ID, Point_ID (the sequence within its array), Row/Col for grids, Bearing for circles, and the usual Stratum, Src_FID and Category fields where they apply.

scriptExample.title: Random Sample Array Generator example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Five 5x5 grid plots at 50 m spacing, at least 500 m apart, each fitting entirely inside the study area, reproducible with a seed.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # strata_method options (matching is by prefix; same as Random Point Generator): # "No stratification (the whole area is one stratum)" # "Stratify by individual polygon" / "... polyline" # "Stratify by raster category (Value field)" # "Stratify by contiguous raster region" # "Stratify by strata ID field" (+ strata_field) # alloc_method options (counts are ARRAYS): # "Fixed total number of arrays" (unstratified) # "Equal count in each stratum" (+ n_per_stratum) # "Count proportional to stratum area" / "... length" # "Count equal to a population field" / "Count proportional to a population field" # "By density (arrays per area unit)" / "... per length unit" # array_shape options: # "Grid (rows and columns of points)" (+ n_rows, n_cols, point_spacing) # "Triangular (a triangular lattice filling a circle)" (+ array_points, point_spacing) # "Circular (points evenly spaced on a circle)" (+ array_points, radius, # randomize_start, include_center) # "Along the polyline (a one-dimensional array of points)" (+ array_points, # point_spacing; polylines only) # orientation_mode: "Fixed orientation angle" / "Random orientation for each array" / # "Align each array to the polyline direction" (polylines only) # spacing_type: "Absolute spatial distance" / "Distance measured along the polyline" / # "Network distance through connected polylines" # linear_units: "Meters" / "Kilometers" / "Feet" / "Miles" arcpy.jenness.RandomSampleArrayGenerator( boundary=r"D:\data\study.gdb\study_area", strata_method="No stratification (the whole area is one stratum)", alloc_method="Fixed total number of arrays", n_arrays=5, array_shape="Grid (rows and columns of points)", n_rows=5, n_cols=5, point_spacing=50.0, orientation_mode="Random orientation for each array", must_fit=True, min_spacing=500.0, linear_units="Meters", random_seed=42, out_fc=r"D:\data\study.gdb\sample_arrays")
